# {{< var workshop.name >}} {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.home-lead}
Applied Replication for Data Skills (AR4DS) is a hands-on workshop that introduces social data science tools and statistical methods through the reanalysis of a published finding. The focal published finding comes from an article reanalysed as part of [SCORE (Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence)](https://www.cos.io/score), a large-scale, multi-method research initiative designed to improve the assessment of scientific credibility in the social and behavioural sciences. Operationalising scientific credibility as the 'repeatability' of research findings, SCORE subjected an initial selection of 600 academic publications to three tests: whether published results can be *reproduced* with the original data and code; to what extent a central finding is *robust* to alternative analytical choices; and whether the finding can be *replicated* using new data.
:::

::: {.home-cta}
[Case studies](#cases) [SCORE](#score)
:::

## Case studies {#the-cases .unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The case studies differ in the statistics and the data handling that they ask for, from a comparison of proportions in one public file of emails to a panel of country-years built from sixteen licensed surveys, and each site offers the formats that its case study allows, with slide decks of its own and a companion of the methods that the case study can teach. Further case studies are in preparation.
:::

:::: {.home-cases}

::: {.home-casecard .home-reveal}
[1]{.home-rung}

### [Housing and racial bias](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/) {#housing-and-racial-bias .unnumbered .unlisted}

In a field experiment published in the *American Journal of Political Science* in 2017, the same short email was sent to about a thousand public housing authorities in the United States, each time signed with one of six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic sender. The claim, in the form in which the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] gave it to its analysts, is that "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, abstract].

<details class="home-more">
<summary>Learning outcomes</summary>

**Reproducible workflows.** Reproducing exactly the four statistics recorded for the robustness study's analysts from the file deposited on the Harvard Dataverse, and tracing the one that a plain chi-square test does not give to a default of the software, the continuity correction; declaring one specification in a short preregistration before running it, and running it again on the data of the replication's new experiment.

**Social data science tools.** R with the datawizard verbs and tinyplot, the models read with parameters and marginaleffects, a causal graph written with dagitty, and a report written in Quarto in an IDE, or the same tasks in the browser through webR.

**Statistical methods.** Proportions and the chi-square test, the linear probability model set against the logit, what conditioning on a reply does to an experiment, randomisation inference and statistical power, and a specification curve of 64 analyses.

</details>

<details class="home-more">
<summary>Prerequisites</summary>

What a first course in quantitative methods teaches: a proportion, a regression and a test of a hypothesis. No R is assumed, since the preparation includes a module on R written for someone who has never programmed, and the part-day format needs nothing but a browser.

</details>

[Go to the case study](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/){.home-go}
:::

::: {.home-casecard .home-reveal}
[2]{.home-rung}

### [Europeanisation and the economy](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/) {#europeanisation-and-the-economy .unnumbered .unlisted}

An article published in the *European Sociological Review* in 2016 drew on Eurobarometer surveys conducted between 2004 and 2013 to examine whether the economic crisis had changed the meanings that citizens attach to the European Union. The claim, in the form in which the robustness study gave it to its analysts, is that "... poor economic performances ... decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 619].

<details class="home-more">
<summary>Learning outcomes</summary>

**Reproducible workflows.** Reproducing the results recorded for three of the robustness study's analysts from panels aggregated from Eurobarometer surveys, reading the terms of use under which GESIS releases the survey files, which forbid passing the files on or processing the files with an AI system, and declaring one of 864 specifications in a short preregistration before running it.

**Social data science tools.** R with the datawizard verbs and fixest, standard errors with few clusters read with parameters, a report written in Quarto in an IDE, or the same tasks in the browser through webR.

**Statistical methods.** Aggregating repeated cross-sections into a panel, fixed and random effects and the within–between model, inference with few clusters, how the scales behind the outcome are built, and a multiverse of 864 specifications.

</details>

<details class="home-more">
<summary>Prerequisites</summary>

What a first course in quantitative methods teaches, including linear regression and its standard errors. No R is assumed, since the preparation includes a module on R written for someone who has never programmed, and the part-day format needs nothing but a browser.

</details>

[Go to the case study](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/){.home-go}
:::

## Formats {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The workshop is taught in three formats, and each workshop's facilitator chooses its format and its case study. Each format is an ordered route through the pages of its case study, with a sidebar of its own and the slide deck that it uses, so that the link that you receive for a workshop leads straight to its route.
:::

:::: {.home-grid}

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### Part-day {#short .unnumbered .unlisted}

[Two halves, in the browser]{.home-meta}

One case study with nothing to install and nothing preregistered, worked on the slides themselves, which run R inside the browser: the claim and the five reanalyses, the estimand statement, the reproduction of one reanalysis of your choice, the menu of analyses and the curve of the claim, and the replication with new data.

[Housing](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/tracks/short/), [Europeanisation](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/tracks/short/).
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### Full-day {#day .unnumbered .unlisted}

[Four parts, in your IDE]{.home-meta}

One case study in four parts, worked in the IDE workspace, while the slides, which run R inside the browser, show each step with its output and stand in for the workspace if an installation fails: the claim and the credibility of social science, the estimand and the causal graph, the reproduction of one reanalysis chosen by each participant, and robustness, with the menu of defensible analyses, the class chart, the curve of the claim and one analysis declared before it runs.

[Housing](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/tracks/day/), [Europeanisation](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/tracks/day/).
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### Self-taught {#independent .unnumbered .unlisted}

[At your own pace, in R]{.home-meta}

Each case study holds a route for a reader who works alone, which takes the case study through the five tasks with the modules of its companion between them and ends on a project of your own.

[Housing](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/tracks/independent/), [Europeanisation](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/tracks/independent/).
:::

## Methods and tools {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The companion of each site holds the methods that arise from its case study, from what its original authors or its five analysts did or from the shape of its data. The estimand and the causal graph, the multiverse and the common scale of the five analysts are taught in every case study, because every exercise rests on them. The tools serve every case study and are taught once, on these pages, with the file of the Housing case study as their running example: the installation and the help page, and the modules on R, the IDE, Quarto, and Git and GitHub, all in the Tools menu. The table maps each case study onto its formats and onto these modules and those of its companion, and each name in the table links to the module that teaches it.
:::

## SCORE {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The claims of the case studies come from the work of SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence, a programme that put claims from published social and behavioural research through three kinds of repetition [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. A reproduction repeats the original analysis on the original data, a robustness check applies different but defensible analyses to the same data, and a replication asks the same question of new data. In the robustness study, 457 analysts produced 504 reanalyses of 100 claims, at least five for each, from the data of the original studies [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136], and the workshop's exercise follows its design on a smaller scale.
:::

:::: {.home-cases .home-reveal}

::: {.home-r}
### [The programme](score.qmd#sec-score) {#score-programme .unnumbered .unlisted}

SCORE and its three studies, of reproducibility, robustness and replicability, and what the record of the programme holds for each case study.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### [The robustness study](score.qmd#sec-robustness) {#the-robustness-article .unnumbered .unlisted}

How the robustness study chose its claims and set its two tasks, how it placed 504 reanalyses on one scale, what that scale assumes, and what its article found.
:::

<!-- The biography is shortened from chrismoreh.com (source: D:/GitHub/chrismoreh-source/index.qmd); CM cut its second paragraph on 2026-11-20. -->

A social scientist interested in the political sociology of migration, mobility, ethnicity and nationalism.

I approach social research as a comparative, interdisciplinary and multimethodological endeavour. My work has combined ethnographic observation, document analysis, survey methods and statistical modelling.

I'm enthusiastic about transparency and reproducibility in the social sciences, and my [pedagogical approach](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/mediav8/library/file-downloads/research-services/open-research/moreh.pdf) seeks to develop skills that facilitate open and credible research practices.

Find me at: [chrismoreh.com](https://chrismoreh.com)

## AI disclosure {.unnumbered}

The workshop grew out of a short session written for an open research conference at Newcastle University, which was built on my own reanalysis of one claim in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. Its extension into the present workshop, with several case studies from SCORE and formats of different lengths, was carried out with the help of three Claude models developed by Anthropic, used through Claude Code and its sub-agents, each model suited to a different kind of work by the strengths that its system card documents. [Claude Opus 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5-system-card), whose system card reports gains in coding, agentic tasks and "long-horizon professional work", suits the long tasks: improving the websites, designing the formats and drafting sections of the text of the pages, the slides and the IDE workspaces. [Claude Fable 5.2](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-5-2-mythos-5-2-system-card), described in its system card as advancing "the frontier in coding, knowledge work, and problem-solving", suits the most demanding checks, of the R code and of the statistical reasoning behind the exercises, and the vetting of software before it is installed. [Claude Sonnet 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-sonnet-5-5-system-card), which its system card finds "broadly less capable than Opus 5.5" while rivalling it in a few areas, suits routine work that is fully specified in advance, such as a change of wording applied across hundreds of files or the search for errors and inconsistencies across the materials. Everything that the models produced is being checked by me for its accuracy and its language.

AI assistants can also help participants during the workshop, with a piece of code that fails or as a partner in generating and testing ideas, used in a way that supports the work of the participant rather than replacing it, which means keeping the judgement of the analysis one's own and saying where the help came from. The module on [AI assistants](tools/ai.qmd) sets out how to use one in the IDE, and its section on [licensed data](tools/ai.qmd#sec-licensed) explains why the files of some case studies, such as the Eurobarometer surveys distributed by GESIS, may not be processed with an AI system at all.
